questions.text: Which PostgreSQL objects are normally represented physically by one or more relation forks?

answers.text: Objects that store data: tables, indexes, sequences, and materialized views
Tables only
Entire databases only
Views and functions only

questions.explanation: For objects that physically store data, PostgreSQL uses relations represented by several forks.

questions.text: Which relation forks exist in PostgreSQL? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: main
fsm
vm
init
wal

questions.explanation: The material covers the main fork, free space map, visibility map, and initialization fork. WAL is not a relation fork from this set.

questions.text: What is stored in a relation's main fork?

answers.text: The actual data: table row versions or index entries
Only free-space information
Only page-visibility information
A backup empty copy of the relation after a crash

questions.explanation: The main fork contains the relation's actual data. It exists for objects that physically store data.

questions.text: Which statements about relation file segments are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A large fork is split into segments
The typical maximum size of one segment is 1 GB
Subsequent segments can have suffixes .1, .2, and so on
Each segment must correspond to a separate SQL table

questions.explanation: As a relation fork grows, it is split into physical segments. The lesson shows files NNN, NNN.1, NNN.2 and a 1 GB segment size.

questions.text: What suffix does a free space map fork file have?

answers.text: _fsm
_vm
_init
_wal

questions.explanation: Free space map files have the suffix _fsm.

source.locator: Storage Page Layout / Free Space Map

questions.text: Which statements about the FSM fork are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It stores free-space information
It helps find pages suitable for placing new data
It can exist for both tables and indexes
It contains the table row versions themselves

questions.explanation: FSM is the free space map. The notes separately emphasize that this fork is used for both tables and indexes.

questions.text: What suffix does a visibility map file have?

answers.text: _vm
_fsm
_init
_visibility

questions.explanation: Visibility map files have the suffix _vm.

questions.text: Which statements about the visibility map are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It is a visibility bitmap
The file for this fork has the suffix _vm
In the model used here, the fork exists for tables
It is the main file containing row versions

questions.explanation: VM stores service information about page visibility and is a separate table fork rather than the main row storage.

questions.text: For which objects is the init fork created?

answers.text: For unlogged tables and their indexes
For all ordinary tables
Only for system catalogs
Only for temporary views

questions.explanation: The initialization fork has the suffix _init and exists for UNLOGGED relations.

questions.text: What is characteristic of unlogged tables and their init fork? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Changes to such tables are not written to WAL in the normal way
They can be faster because ordinary WAL logging is absent
After a crash, the main fork can be restored from the init fork state
The init fork is intended to store current user rows during normal operation

questions.explanation: Init represents the initial empty state of an unlogged relation and is used after a crash because the contents of an UNLOGGED table cannot be recovered from WAL.

questions.text: What restriction on a row version creates the need for TOAST?

answers.text: A row version must fit on one page
A row cannot contain more than one text field
A row must always fit in one 1-GB segment
All variable-length values must be stored separately

questions.explanation: TOAST solves the problem of large values under the requirement that a row version must physically fit on a single page.

questions.text: What actions can PostgreSQL apply to large values through TOAST? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Compress the value
Move the value to a separate TOAST table
Compress first and then move it out if necessary
Move the entire database to another tablespace

questions.explanation: The material lists compression, out-of-line storage, and a combination of the two as ways to reduce the size of the main row version.

questions.text: In which schema are ordinary TOAST tables stored?

answers.text: pg_toast
public
pg_catalog
information_schema

questions.explanation: When needed, a service TOAST table is created for the main table in the pg_toast schema.

questions.text: Which statements about TOAST tables are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It has its own index
Large values are stored in it as fragments
Access to it is transparent to the application
It replaces the main fork of the original table

questions.explanation: A TOAST table is an auxiliary relation: it contains fragments of long values, is served by an index, and is used transparently by PostgreSQL.

questions.text: What happens to an already out-of-line TOAST value if UPDATE creates a new main-row version but the long field itself does not change?

answers.text: The new row version can reference the same TOAST value
The TOAST value must always be fully duplicated
The field is automatically replaced with NULL
The entire TOAST table is recreated

questions.explanation: TOAST has independent versioning. If the long value did not change, the new main-row version can continue referencing the existing value, saving space.

source.locator: TOAST and reuse of unchanged values

questions.text: Which PostgreSQL functions can determine the sizes of relations and related objects? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: pg_relation_size
pg_table_size
pg_indexes_size
pg_total_relation_size
pg_database_size

questions.explanation: The material successively covers the size of an individual fork, a table with TOAST, indexes, and the full relation size. `pg_database_size` measures a database, not a relation or related objects from this list.

questions.text: What does pg_table_size show for a regular table?

answers.text: The size of the table together with its TOAST part, excluding the table's regular indexes
Only the size of the main fork
Only the total size of all regular indexes
The full size of the entire database

questions.explanation: pg_table_size includes the table itself and its TOAST part with the TOAST index, but not the ordinary indexes of the main table.

questions.text: Which function-to-result mappings are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: pg_relation_size — size of the selected relation fork
pg_indexes_size — total size of the table's regular indexes
pg_total_relation_size — full size of the table including its indexes
pg_indexes_size — size of the entire database including WAL

questions.explanation: Each function has its own scope: an individual fork, indexes, or a full relation with dependent structures.

questions.text: For an UNLOGGED table, the presence of which file confirms that its initialization fork exists?

answers.text: A file with the _init suffix
A file with the _vm suffix
A file with the _fsm suffix
A file with the _toast suffix

questions.explanation: The exercise asks you to create an unlogged table and directly verify the presence of the init fork, whose file has the _init suffix.

questions.text: Which actions can be used to investigate TOAST behavior for a text column? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Create a table with a text column
Determine the storage strategy of that column
Change the strategy to external and insert short and long values
Inspect the TOAST table with a direct query and explain the result
Restart the PostgreSQL server before inspecting the TOAST table

questions.explanation: The exercise connects storage-strategy configuration with observing which values actually end up in the TOAST table. Restarting the server is not one of the listed exercise steps.
